title: System Design Primer ⭐️: How to start with distributed systems?

best.what: pizza-shop analogy for vertical/horizontal scaling and avoiding a single point of failure by adding backups

why: Genuinely teen-friendly thanks to the pizza-shop analogy, but it's building up to scaling for millions of orders across distributed shops - way past what a 15-user Sheets app needs; good 'how do big websites work' literacy, not a building skill they'll use.

title: System Design BASICS: Horizontal vs. Vertical Scaling
why: Opens with a decent 60-second API/request/response recap but then becomes a dry, jargon-heavy comparison table (RPC vs IPC, data consistency, hardware limits) aimed at interview answers; the Primer video covers the same ground with a far better analogy.

title: What is LOAD BALANCING? ⚖️
why: A whiteboard-math walkthrough of hashing requests mod N servers and rebalancing buckets when a server is added - real consistent-hashing math, not something a 14-15 year old vibe-coding a Sheets app needs.

title: What is CONSISTENT HASHING and Where is it used?
why: No captions (nocaps) - judged by title only. Consistent hashing is core distributed-systems/interview material, unrelated to the course.

title: What is a MESSAGE QUEUE and Where is it used?

best.what: pizza-order queue analogy for asynchronous processing: taking the order immediately instead of making the customer wait for the pizza to finish

why: The queue-of-pizza-orders analogy for asynchronous processing is genuinely followable and relatable, but message queues (RabbitMQ/Kafka, heartbeat failover) aren't something they'll touch in Apps Script; fine as a 'how big apps stay responsive' bonus.

title: What is a MICROSERVICE ARCHITECTURE and what are its advantages?
why: Explicitly framed as interview prep ('what would happen in a system design interview') comparing monolith vs. microservices trade-offs for large teams and big companies - not relevant to a single Apps Script project.

title: What is DATABASE SHARDING?
why: Sharding, hierarchical shards, consistent hashing, master-slave failover for databases - real distributed-database engineering, nowhere near a 15-user Sheet.

title: Caching in distributed systems: A friendly introduction

best.what: Instagram newsfeed example: why repeating the same database work is wasteful and how caching cuts response time from 220ms to a few ms
what happens on a cache miss and why cached data can go stale (eventual consistency)

why: Exactly the 'caching as why apps feel fast' kind of video the brief points at - concrete example, plain-language trade-offs between speed and freshness, and Apps Script even has its own CacheService the teacher can tie this to.

title: What is a CDN (Content Delivery Network)?

best.what: why one server can't be fast for everyone in the world, and how spreading copies of content closer to users (a CDN) fixes it

why: Short, clear and relatable ('why does a video load slowly from far away'), but it explicitly assumes you've already watched the caching and distributed-systems videos - a fun bonus on 'how the web works', not something they'll build.

title: What is the Publisher Subscriber Model?
why: Message brokers (Kafka/RabbitMQ), a bank-transfer consistency failure scenario, idempotency - solid distributed-systems teaching but well past a Sheets-backed app.

title: What's an Event Driven System?
why: Event buses, replay-from-log debugging, at-least/at-most-once delivery guarantees; the Counter-Strike lag-compensation aside is fun but buried in otherwise advanced architecture content.

title: What is an API and how do you design it? 🗒️✅

best.what: what an API actually is (a documented contract, not how the code works), naming functions honestly, why extra parameters/fields are bad design, and how to think about error cases

why: This is the exact 'what is an API' video the brief flags as core material - a clear WhatsApp-admins example, naming and error-design advice a kid designing their own Apps Script functions can actually use; the last third (HTTP routing, pagination/fragmentation, financial atomicity) is more advanced.

title: System Design Walkthrough at InterviewReady - Designed for SDE 1 to SDE 3 Interview Preparation
why: Pure marketing/UI walkthrough of the paid interview-prep course website (login, coupon codes, course sections) - not a teaching video at all.

title: Introduction to NoSQL databases

best.what: SQL's rigid columns vs. NoSQL's flexible JSON blob - why adding a new field doesn't require an 'ALTER TABLE'

why: The opening SQL-vs-NoSQL schema comparison is a fair teacher talking point for why a Sheet's rows don't need a fixed schema, but 20+ minutes of the video is Cassandra internals (quorum, SSTables, gossip protocol, hash rings) that no kid needs.

title: System Design: TINDER as a microservice architecture
why: A full mock system-design interview (blob vs. file storage, XMPP, distributed file systems, sharded recommendation engine) for a dating app at Tinder's scale - none of it transfers to a 15-user Apps Script game.

title: Designing INSTAGRAM: System Design of News Feed

best.what: designing the likes/comments/follows tables step by step, including why you don't just bolt a 'likes count' column onto the posts table

why: The table-design segment for likes, comments and follows is a real, transferable database-design lesson (same spirit as the Database Star videos), but it's wrapped in a full mock interview covering load balancers, cache snapshots and celebrity fan-out that's out of scope.

title: WHATSAPP System Design: Chat Messaging Systems for Interviews

best.what: why chat can't just use normal request/response, and how the sent/delivered/read tick marks actually work

why: This is the brief's own example of a fun bonus - 'how does WhatsApp deliver a message' explains the tick marks kids see every day - but it's framed as a full interview answer and the back half (consistent hashing for groups, message queues, idempotency) needs a guide.

title: How NETFLIX onboards new content: Video Processing at scale 🎥

best.what: why Netflix stores each video in many formats/resolutions and chops it into scene-based chunks instead of buffering the whole file

why: A fun, concrete case study kids can relate to (why streaming doesn't buffer, why quality changes) - a good 'how the web works' bonus, though CDN/ISP-box jargon (Open Connect, S3) needs a little unpacking.

title: Capacity Planning and Estimation: How much data does YouTube store daily?
why: A Fermi-estimation drill for system-design interviews (how much data does YouTube store per day) - interview technique, not a concept the course needs.

title: How databases scale writes: The power of the log ✍️🗒️
why: B+ trees vs. log-structured merge trees, SSTable compaction, bloom filters - real database-internals engineering, far beyond a Sheets-backed app.

title: Distributed Consensus and Data Replication strategies on the server
why: Master-slave replication, split-brain, two-phase commit, MVCC, the Saga pattern, plus a sponsored plug for an interview-prep product - squarely interview/distributed-systems material.

title: Designing a location database: QuadTrees and Hilbert Curves
why: A genuinely interesting data-structures deep dive (fractals, Hilbert curves) for location search at scale, but it's advanced CS, not app-building material for these kids.

title: Data Consistency and Tradeoffs in Distributed Systems
why: CAP-theorem trade-offs and a full two-phase-commit protocol walkthrough - core distributed-systems theory, not applicable here.

title: System Design Interview: TikTok architecture with @sudoCODE
why: No captions (nocaps) - judged by title only. A 45-minute mock system-design interview for TikTok's architecture; explicitly interview-prep content.

title: 5 Tips for System Design Interviews
why: No captions (nocaps) - judged by title only. Interview tips, not course content.

title: How to avoid a single point of failure in distributed systems ✅
why: No captions (nocaps) - judged by title only. Distributed-systems reliability concept, off-topic for the course.
